Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:57: Likewise, one of the forty-eight things through which Torah is acquired is the acceptance of sufferings (Avot 6:6), and the acceptance of sufferings is the matter of Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon, who accepted sufferings upon himself (Bava Metzia 84b). In a similar manner, a person must afflict himself through mortification of eating, sleeping, and pleasure, or by fasting, and the like.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:58: In Tanna Devei Eliyahu it says that whoever accepts sufferings is saved from Gehinnom and enters Gan Eden, in these words: this is what Scripture says (Lamentations 3:27), "it is good for a man that he bear the yoke in his youth." Elijah, of blessed memory, said, happy is he who accepts sufferings from his youth, for his end will be at ease. From where do we know this? From Job, for so his companions said to him (Job 8:7), "and though your beginning was small, your end shall greatly increase" — and not only that, but the sufferings upon you shall save you from Gehinnom and place you in Gan Eden, as it is said (ibid. 36:16), "and He also would have led you out of the mouth of distress into a broad place, where there is no constraint beneath it, and the rest of your table would be full of fatness." Rabbi Acha said in the name of Rabbi Yonah: his companions said to Job, even though the Adversary incited the Holy One, blessed be He, against you, as it is said (ibid. 2:3), "and you incited Me against him, to destroy him without cause" — the Holy One, blessed be He, desires to save you "from the mouth of distress" — from Gehinnom, whose mouth is narrow above and it is broad below, as it is said, "broad, with no constraint beneath it" — this teaches that Gehinnom has no foundation, neither of earth nor of stone, so that the wicked have no rest in it. And how are they judged within it? Its force flings them like birds, light and diminished from every side, until they become like a hair's breadth, as it is said (Psalms 49:15), "and their form shall wear away, Sheol being their dwelling," and it is written (Job 10:22), "a land of gloom, like thick darkness" — from here you learn that they stand in it like a bird standing in the air. And it is not enough that sufferings saved you from Gehinnom, but they also brought you into Gan Eden, as it is said, "and the rest of your table would be full of fatness"; therefore Scripture says (Lamentations 3:27), "it is good for a man that he bear the yoke in his youth." — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:59: Know that although sufferings are the power of judgment against a person, and it would appear as though they flow from Gevurah, this is not so — for they come only from the side of Chesed, as it is written (Psalms 103:8), "merciful and gracious," etc., "slow to anger and abundant in kindness," and it is written (ibid. 103:10), "He has not dealt with us according to our sins," etc., and it is written (Proverbs 3:12), "for whom the Lord loves, He rebukes," and it is written (ibid. 13:24), "he who withholds his rod hates his son, but he who loves him disciplines him early." And there is no love except from the side of Chesed.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:60: This is because the soul is the daughter of Abraham our father, peace be upon him, as explained in the Sabba [Zohar] (parashat Mishpatim 95a), regarding "and if a priest's daughter is married to a strange man" (Leviticus 22:12), for the soul is called "a priest's daughter," and it says, in these words: "a priest's daughter" — this is the supernal soul, the first daughter of Abraham our father to converts, and He draws this soul from a supernal place. — end of quotation. And so it is explained there (96b) regarding (Exodus 21:8), "to a foreign people he shall have no power to sell her, since he has dealt deceitfully with her" — that this garment is her precious separation-garment from the side of Chesed, called "Eloha"; see there, in these words: the Holy One, blessed be He, marks her and seals her with a single seal of His own precious garment, and what is this? The Holy Name called "Eloha," and this is "as in the days of Eloha He watched over me." — end of quotation, as pertains here.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:61: Since the soul flows from the side of Chesed, its purification too is from the side of Chesed; and if, Heaven forbid, it becomes impure, just as the priest would purify the metzora, as it is written (Leviticus 14:2), "on the day of his purification, he shall be brought to the priest," so the soul is purified through the fire of Gehinnom, to be refined, and afterward it is elevated through Michael, who is the supernal priest who offers up the souls of the righteous, as our sages, of blessed memory, explained (Chagigah 12b; Menachot 110a, see Tosafot s.v. "and Michael"). And so it is explained in the Zohar (parashat Metzora 53b), in these words: afterward it is judged in several judgments. And the explanation of "afterward" follows the wording of the passage stated there, which recounted the matter of the soul's departure from the body, and it says: afterward it was judged in several judgments, until it remained in Gehinnom through the agency of Dumah, and the body is judged in the grave until it returns to dust, and the soul is in the fire of Gehinnom under several judgments, until that time it has accepted its punishment for being distanced from the place where the righteous dwell; after it has accepted its punishment and its time to be purified arrives, then it ascends from Gehinnom and is refined of its sin like iron refined in fire, and they ascend with it until it enters the lower Garden of Eden, and it is washed there in those waters, and washed in the perfumes there, in the manner it says, "perfumed with myrrh and frankincense," and then they ascend with it until it is brought near as an offering upon the altar — this being what is written (Leviticus 14:2), "this shall be the law of the metzora, on the day of his purification, he shall be brought to the priest" — the supernal priest above; this soul, which was not too greatly defiled in this world, has rectification of this kind; but if not, "that which is crooked cannot be made straight." — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:62: Here, the end result of the soul's offering is through the priest, and even though it enters Gehinnom and the fire purifies it, the intent is that it be refined and purified so that the power of Chesed, a white light, may shine within it — from whence the soul flowed, as we explained.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:63: We find, in this aspect, that the Holy One, blessed be He, performs kindness with the soul in washing it of its stains in order to give good reward — this being (Psalms 139:10), "even there Your hand shall lead me" — to purify the soul, "and Your right hand shall hold me" — to give it good reward.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:64: This is like the parable of a mother washing her child of his filth, thereby performing kindness with him — for if she left him in his filth, it would be cruel, as his body would deteriorate; and although the child cries and suffers, it is all for his own good. Likewise the father who strikes his son and disciplines him with the rod performs an act of lovingkindness, doing good for his soul so that it not descend to Gehinnom — for it is better that he suffer a small distress than a great distress, which is the fire of Gehinnom, continual day and night, the soul's suffering not ceasing until it is purified. So too the Holy One, blessed be He, in this world exacts payment from the righteous and disciplines them with the rod of suffering little by little, so that they not descend to Gehinnom — but not so with the wicked, for if they were disciplined with sufferings, they would add transgression to transgression.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:65: Therefore, whoever the Holy One, blessed be He, loves, He disciplines little by little, as our sages, of blessed memory, explained (Avodah Zarah 4a) on the verse (Amos 3:2), "only you have I known of all the families of the earth, therefore I will punish you for all your iniquities" — they said there this is like a parable of a man who is a creditor to two people, one whom he loves and one whom he hates — from the one he loves, he collects little by little; from the one he hates, he collects everything all at once.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:66: It follows that there are two kinds of suffering: the first is from the side of Chesed, called "sufferings of love," collected little by little — these are sufferings that do not involve the nullification of Torah and prayer — in the manner our sages, of blessed memory, said (Pesachim 118a) on the verse (Psalms 118:1), "give thanks to the Lord, for He is good, for His kindness is forever" — in these words: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said, give thanks to Him who collects a person's debt in a beneficial manner: from the rich man, through his ox; from the poor man, through his lamb; from the orphan, through his egg; from the widow, through her hen. — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:67: There are also sufferings that are not of love, which do involve the nullification of Torah and prayer, in which the judgment is poured out all together at once — and this resembles somewhat the fire of Gehinnom, which purifies the soul all at once, without giving it any respite or relief in between.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:68: These two aspects are the two aspects found within the attributes, as explained in the Zohar in parashat Va'era — either the general aspect of Gevurah within Chesed, or Chesed within Gevurah. What is the general aspect of Gevurah within Chesed is sufferings of love, where Chesed dominates and the judgment is poured out little by little; and what is the general aspect of Chesed within Gevurah, and Gevurah dominates, is sufferings that are not of love. But there is never any suffering in which the aspect of Chesed does not partake, to purify and refine, as we explained through the parable of the mother washing her child, and so it is written (Isaiah 4:4), "if the Lord has washed away the filth of the daughters of Zion." He was precise in spelling this Name with an aleph-dalet [Adonai, the mercy-aspect], and you will find good reason in my words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:69: It follows that whoever accepts sufferings upon himself becomes a chariot for Chesed — for Chesed, which is the priest, is called "a pure man," as explained in parashat Chukat — and this is because through sufferings he purifies his soul and draws it near to Chesed.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:70: For this reason, one who sits in a fast is called a chasid, as our sages, of blessed memory, explained (Ta'anit 11b), on the verse (Proverbs 11:17), "the pious man rewards his own soul" — for through the heating of his fat and blood, diminished through the fire of the fast, he purifies his soul and refines it and draws it near to Chesed — and this is a judgment he accepts little by little, for at night he eats and is sustained from the flow of Chesed, from which food flows, as explained in the Gate of Holiness, chapter 15.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:71: Likewise, any suffering a person accepts upon himself that does not involve the nullification of Torah and prayer — such as diminishing his food, or sitting in a fast for a certain number of hours in the day, as Rabbi Yochanan used to do, as explained in Tractate Keritot regarding "swears to his own hurt and does not change" (Psalms 15:4) — such as Rabbi Yochanan, who would say, I shall be in a fast until I reach home. And in the Yerushalmi, chapter Konam (Nedarim, ch. 8, halachah 1), it states the words of Rabbi Yochanan: one may fast for [part of] hours, for Rabbi Yochanan said, I hereby am in a fast until I finish my [Torah] chapter, until I finish my [weekly Torah] portion. — end of quotation. Similar to this are sufferings of love, where a person does to himself what it would be fitting for the Holy One, blessed be He, to do to him out of love.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:72: However, this aspect of accepting sufferings upon oneself out of love applies correctly if he has not sinned so greatly that his punishment is to descend to Gehinnom; but if he sinned in the matter of forbidden sexual relations and the like, which is of the third category that Rabbi Yishmael enumerated regarding the four categories of atonement we explained above — for if he transgressed a negative commandment requiring sufferings to scour away, as it is written (Psalms 89:33), "then I will punish their transgression with the rod, and their iniquity with plagues" — for surely those sufferings are with plagues, and involve the nullification of Torah and prayer, by this reasoning.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:73: The reason the Holy One, blessed be He, gives him harsh sufferings is that the Holy One, blessed be He, has no desire for his Torah at such a time, since his soul is greatly defiled with the filth of his sins; and without doubt, if sufferings did not come upon him, he would know that the Holy One, blessed be He, hates him and is holding him in reserve to consign everything together to Gehinnom. Therefore he must accept harsh sufferings upon himself, even if they involve the nullification of Torah and prayer — for a little Torah with a soul clean of the filth and foul odor of sins is better than much Torah with a soul full of filth, and of him it is written (Psalms 50:16), "but to the wicked, God says, what right have you to declare My statutes," etc.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:74: There are already sins that, although they are not among those liable to excision mentioned in the Torah, our sages, of blessed memory, explained that they are equal in weight to them — for slander is equal to idolatry, forbidden sexual relations, and bloodshed (Arachin 15b), and likewise anger is equal to idolatry, and pride is equal to denying the fundamental principle [of faith] (see Sotah 4b) — and without doubt one must accept sufferings until purified.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:75: In any case, whatever a person accepts in this world, even if it involves the nullification of Torah and prayer, all of it is on the side of Chesed, and the little he accepts upon himself is greatly valued before Him, as it is written (Psalms 103:10), "He has not dealt with us according to our sins, nor rewarded us according to our iniquities" — for the world is conducted according to Chesed, as it is written (ibid. 89:3), "I said, the world shall be built with kindness." However, after the soul's departure from this world, it is judged according to strict, complete judgment, without leniency of even a single point, as we explained above, that the World to Come is given only through sufferings, as it is written (Proverbs 6:23), "and the way of life is the reproofs of discipline" — the meaning of "the way of life" being the supernal life, the life of the World to Come, which requires the "reproofs of discipline" — for in order to merit that supernal pleasantness, this "surely" and "would that" are needed, for that pleasantness is given only to those who fear Him and His pious ones, as it is written (Psalms 31:20), "how great is Your goodness, which You have hidden away for those who fear You," and it is written (ibid. 36:8), "how precious is Your kindness, O God," etc., "let the pious exult in glory" (ibid. 149:5).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:76: Therefore, threefold sufferings are needed — "reproofs" [plural, two], "discipline" [singular, one], totaling three — for the World to Come encompasses two grades along with it, which are Torah and the Land of Israel; therefore he is given doubled sufferings, namely according to complete, strict precision, without leniency in anything. Regarding Torah and the Land of Israel, sufferings are mentioned only once: in Torah (Psalms 94:12), "happy is the man whom You discipline, O Lord, and teach him from Your Torah"; and likewise regarding the Land of Israel (Deuteronomy 8:5), "as a man disciplines his son," etc. — all of these are sufferings with mercy: in Torah, the Name Yah is mentioned, which is mercy; and likewise regarding the Land of Israel, "the Lord your God" — the name of mercy is shared with judgment. But in the World to Come, neither the name of mercy nor of judgment is mentioned, to indicate complete judgment — YHVH cannot be mentioned without indicating mercy; Elohim cannot be mentioned, since in the entire Book of Proverbs "Elohim" is not mentioned (except in three places), for the reason explained in the Zohar (parashat Bo, beginning of p. 39), that Proverbs corresponds to the central line; see there. Therefore it mentions doubled sufferings, because it could not mention "Elohim."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:77: This suffices as an exhortation for the discerning person, to arouse his heart to repentance and to know how to purify his soul from its afflictions — for there is nothing more precious to a man than his own soul, and each person knows the blemishes of his own soul; therefore, while time is still given him, let him heal himself with the remedies of repentance that will be explained, with God's help, for each and every sin, the purification needed for it, before the regret that will no longer avail.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:78: Having explained the need for suffering for the purification of sin, we must explain that a person must accept them out of love, and this in two aspects. First, that out of love for the Shechinah, he accepts those sufferings upon himself — the reason being that the sinner causes the Shechinah to be struck through him, in the manner of "a foolish son is his mother's grief," which we explained in the Gate of Fear (ch. 9); therefore, out of love for the Shechinah, who is his mother, he says in his heart, better that I be struck in my own body than that my mother be struck.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:79: Further, in another aspect: when a person sins, the Shechinah departs from him, and it is in order that the Shechinah not depart from him that he accepts sufferings upon himself — and so it is explained in the Zohar (parashat Vayechi 245a), in these words: another interpretation, "jealousy is as harsh as Sheol" — just as Sheol, at the time the wicked descend into it, they are informed of their sins, for what reason they descend there, and it is harsh for them — so whoever is jealous [i.e., the attribute of jealousy/zeal] demands [payment] for one's sins, and reckons several deeds, and then the bond of love is bound to him. — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:80: The explanation of "demands [payment] for one's sins" is that sin is the cause of separating love between him and the Shechinah, as it is said (Isaiah 59:2), "but rather your iniquities have separated between you and your God"; and since this lover does not wish his beloved to be separated from him, he himself becomes the creditor who demands his own debt and confesses his sin to his beloved, saying to her, truly I have sinned against you, do not separate from me because of my sin. And since a person confesses, the powers of judgment stay away from him, as explained in the Zohar, parashat Pinchas (231a), and then his judgment is not handed over into the hand of the outside forces, but rather the Holy One, blessed be He, and His Shechinah judge him and discipline him by the hand of holy judgment in this world, as it is said (Jeremiah 10:24), "discipline me, O Lord, but with judgment, not in Your anger," etc., and so David the king, peace be upon him, said (Psalms 54:3), "and in Your might judge me" — the intent being that his judgment be handed over into the hand of the supernal Gevurah, which is holy judgment, and this is with mercy from the side of His mercy, blessed be He, and that he not be handed over into the hand of the outside forces in Gehinnom, which is an evil strap, the blow of a cruel one. And the demand of the debt is the demand of suffering for his sins in this world, so that no claim remains for the accuser, who is his own creditor, to collect his debt from him in Gehinnom — and he says to his soul, such and such you have done, such and such you shall suffer.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:81: As for what is said, "and reckons several deeds" — the explanation is several good deeds to purify his soul, and so that his beloved not distance herself from him, and so that she come to dwell with him, he performs whatever deeds are in his power to find favor in her eyes, that she be reconciled with him.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:82: He says, "and then the bond of love is bound to him" — that he accepts the sufferings out of love, and likewise performs the commandments out of love of the Shechinah, and this is the purpose of love.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:83: In the Zohar (parashat Mishpatim 109b), they explained that repentance, prayer, and accepting sufferings upon oneself help so that one need not come into reincarnation, according to the view of our sages, of blessed memory, mentioned above, in these words: "I love my master..." [Exodus 21:5] — and through an abundance of prayers he loved the Holy One, blessed be He, and rectified his deeds and said, "I love my master, my wife and my children, I will not go out free." And the Holy One, blessed be He, received him in that repentance and that abundance of prayers — what did the Holy One, blessed be He, do? What He had been ready to do — to return him via reincarnation and have him bear punishments in this world for what he did — He did not return him to this world; instead, what did He do to him? He brought him near to the court of the supernal academy, and they judge him and hand him over to the house of lashes, and the Holy One, blessed be He, marks how he was handed over to the house of punishment, and blemishes him to be under the dominion of the Jubilee until a known time, and afterward redeems him. — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 3:84: The reason for this may be said to be that a penitent, in accepting sufferings upon himself, accepts the supernal judgment, and the attributes that purify from blemish and their judgment — and through this he draws his soul near to Chesed, called "the end of the right," and therefore he merits that his soul rest at the end of the right and not return in reincarnation, in the manner that this matter was announced to Daniel (Daniel 12:13), "but you, go your way until the end, and you shall rest and stand in your lot at the end of days [right]."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 4:1: After having explained, in the previous chapter, the need for a penitent to have sufferings to purify his sins, we thought it fit to attach this chapter to it, explaining the matter of fasting, which is needed for a penitent, as explained through the prophet Joel, peace be upon him (Joel 2:12), "return to Me with all your heart, and with fasting and with weeping and with mourning" — the verse begins "with all your heart," which has an etnachta [pause note], and afterward it says "and with fasting and with weeping and with mourning" — the intent being that the essential prerequisite before fasting and weeping is that repentance be from the heart and the soul.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 4:2: Rabbeinu Bachya, the pious author of Chovot HaLevavot, explained four conditions regarding repentance, in these words: chapter 4 — but the boundaries of repentance are four: first, regret over past sins; second, that he abandon them and turn away from them; third, that he confess them and seek forgiveness for them; fourth, that he accept upon his soul, in his innermost being, not to repeat them. — end of quotation. Now, the totality of these four is what is said, "with all your heart" — for when a person performs repentance with a whole heart, these four conditions mentioned are surely included.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 4:3: It is also possible to give another reason: that at times a person is ill or in a place of danger, and he contemplates repentance in his heart, that when he is able he will fast and perform repentance — as we say (Ta'anit 8b), in the days of Rabbi Zeira a decree was issued, and it was decreed that they should not sit in a fast; Rabbi Zeira said to them, let us accept it upon ourselves, and when the decree is annulled, let us sit in it. They said to him, from where do you derive this? He said to them, as it is written (Daniel 10:12), "and he said to me, do not fear, Daniel, for from the first day that you set your heart to understand and to afflict yourself... your words were heard." Here it is explicitly stated that the acceptance of a fast, even though one cannot [yet] fast, avails as though he had actually fasted — and this is "with all your heart."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 4:4: Fasting is needed for the penitent, because through eating the heart grows haughty and comes to rebel, as we quoted in the Gate of Holiness, chapter 15, that a person rebels only through eating and drinking, as it is said (Deuteronomy 11:15-16), "and you shall eat and be satisfied — beware for yourselves," etc., and "and the people sat to eat and drink, and rose up to make merry" (Exodus 32:6), and many similar verses. The essence of fasting is subjugation, as David the king, peace be upon him, said in the psalm of repentance (Psalms 51:19), "the sacrifices of God are a broken spirit," as we explained above (ch. 3).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 4:5: It is further explained in the Zohar (parashat Pinchas 240a), in these words: Rabbi Abba opened, "the sacrifices of God are a broken spirit" — this verse has already been established, that the will of the Holy One, blessed be He, does not desire the offering of a person for his sin, but rather a broken spirit; but people do not know what they are saying. And so I heard from the holy lamp [Rabbi Shimon]: when a person comes to be defiled through his sins, a spirit from the side of impurity is drawn upon him, and it grows haughty over the person and rules over all his desires. When a person comes to purify himself — at the time the Temple stood, he would offer his sacrifice, and all his atonement depended on this: that he regret and break that spirit from within his haughtiness, and subdue it, and this is the breaking of that impure grade. And when that impure spirit is broken and his sacrifice is accepted, this is what is accepted with proper favor; and if this spirit is not broken, his sacrifice is worth nothing, and is handed over to the dogs — for that sacrifice does not belong to the Holy One, blessed be He, but is [as though offered] to dogs. Therefore, "the sacrifices of God are a broken spirit" properly — a broken spirit, that that impure spirit be broken and not rule; and therefore whoever properly breaks it, of him it is written (Psalms 78:39), "a spirit that goes and does not return" — that man shall be in security, and it shall never return to him — this being what is written, "and does not return." "A broken and contrite heart" — that man who did not grow haughty and did not delight in the delights of the world — "O God, You will not despise" — with honor is he toward Him. — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 4:6: Here it is explicitly stated that when the sinner draws upon himself a spirit from the Sitra Achra [Other Side], his heart then grows haughty over him, and the essential sacrifice is a broken spirit, to break that outside spirit, in the manner of breaking the shell of a walnut. And he explains at the end of the passage how the spirit is broken — through the breaking of the heart, namely, that he not grow haughty nor delight in the delights of the world; and through fasting he distances himself from the world's pleasures, and then he breaks that outside spirit.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 4:7: They further explained this matter (Ra'aya Meheimna, parashat Pinchas 247a) in the passage itself, in the explanation of the verse "fine flour for a meal offering" — they say, of blessed memory: YHVH is the central column, its fine flour is the lower Shechinah, its light is fine flour clean of its two sides, without the blemish of darkness and without any admixture of darkness at all — for these darknesses accompany the lights, for chaff and straw preceded [wheat]; and through Israel's sins, darknesses are mixed with lights, and just as a person threshes grain and then sorts it, sorting food from refuse, so Israel must do with their spirit when darkness has become mixed within them — and the secret of the matter is (Psalms 51:19), "the sacrifices of God are a broken spirit" — for thus the darkness, which is the evil inclination, is broken, that which covers over the spirit like chaff covering wheat, like a cloud covering the sun and not letting it shine; and at times the darkness, which is the evil inclination, covers over the good inclination, which is light, and it is as one imprisoned in a house of confinement of spirit — and likewise, when the good inclination is captive in the domain of the evil inclination, likewise the hosts of the good inclination are captive in the domain of the hosts of the evil inclination. And at the time a person breaks his spirit, in all his limbs, before YHVH, what is written? "Saying to the prisoners, go out; to those who are in darkness, reveal yourselves" (Isaiah 49:9). But the Shechinah is clean fine flour, in which no darkness or invalidity can mix. — end of quotation.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 4:8: Here, in this passage, the matter is explained further — that through sin, light becomes mixed with darkness, and that darkness covers over the spirit like a cloud covering the sun, and this is what the verse says (ibid. 59:2), "but rather your iniquities have separated between you and your God" — that they are a partition. So too they said in the Tikkunim (109a), that these kelipot cause separation between the Holy One, blessed be He, and Israel, and this is the secret of "but rather your iniquities have separated between you and your God." — end of quotation. And so it says above this (108b), that these kelipot are a partition between Israel and their Father in Heaven.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 4:9: Since a person sins, through his sin he strengthens the kelipah and thickens the partition, making it like a partition of iron, in the manner of (Isaiah 5:18), "woe to those who draw iniquity with cords of vanity, and sin as with a cart-rope" — and there is no remedy until he breaks the kelipah through fasting, weeping, and mourning, as will be explained, in such a manner that he breaks his spirit and his limbs before YHVH, as it says, "and at the time a person breaks his spirit in all his limbs before YHVH" — and there is no way to break all his limbs and his spirit except through the mortification of fasting, whereby his fat and blood, which are the essence of all the limbs, are diminished and mortified. And just as through eating and drinking his strength grew haughty, and covered the chaff and straw, which are darkness, over the supernal light of his soul, and the spark of the Shechinah too, which was clothed in that darkness — so he mortifies himself without eating, in order to subdue himself and separate the light from the darkness.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 4:10: Especially Torah scholars need to fast, in order to subdue their bodies — for the soul does not shine until the body and its powers are subdued, as they said in the Zohar (parashat Toldot 140b): and come and see, at the time the Holy One, blessed be He, desires his soul, to give it pleasure, He strikes the body so that the soul may rule — for as long as the soul is with the body, it cannot rule; and when the body is broken, the soul rules. — end of quotation. And so they elaborated at length also in the Zohar (parashat Vayeshev 180b); see there. Therefore one must fast, in order to strengthen the power of the soul and weaken matter and its pleasures.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Repentance 4:11: We have already explained in the Gate of Holiness that the breaking of pleasures is like the breaking of the hard shell of a walnut, and it is said in the Tikkunim (69a-b) that the heart is like a walnut, in these words: further, the heart is a walnut — whoever breaks the shell, which is the evil inclination, of it is said (Psalms 51:19), "a broken and contrite heart, O God, You will not despise" — but the haughtiness of a heart that is whole with its shells and is not broken, of it is said (Proverbs 16:5), "an abomination to the Lord is every haughty heart," and the Shechinah does not rest upon him, and from the side of the kelipot people are called "uncircumcised of heart." — end of quotation.
